title: Löwenmensch (Lion-Man of Hohlenstein-Stadel)
originLocation: Hohlenstein-Stadel Cave, Lonetal, Baden-Württemberg, Germany
creator: Unknown Aurignacian ivory carver
anatomy: Cave lion head with alert rounded ears and muzzle
Upright bipedal human torso and legs
Seven parallel transverse incisions across the left upper arm
description: Carved from a single woolly mammoth tusk using flint stone tools, the 31.1-centimeter Hohlenstein-Stadel figurine is the oldest known zoomorphic-human sculpture in the archaeological record. Combining the head of a European cave lion (Panthera spelaea) with an erect human posture, it offers the earliest material evidence of mythic imagination, shamanic transformation, and supernatural hybridity.

title: Jasper Cylinder Seal with Serpopards and Lion-Headed Eagles
originLocation: Southern Mesopotamia (likely Uruk), Iraq
creator: Unknown Uruk glyptic master
anatomy: Muscular feline bodies with elongated, intertwining serpentine necks
Tufted lion tails curving symmetrically overhead
Heraldic lion-headed eagles hovering above the intertwined beasts
description: Cut in deep intaglio from polished jasper during Mesopotamia's first urban revolution, this monumental cylinder seal yields a continuous frieze of confronted 'serpopards' whose sinuous necks entwine in perfect symmetry. Above their backs hover early lion-headed raptors, pairing two foundational composite monsters of archaic Near Eastern cosmology.

title: Temple Lintel Relief of Imdugud (Anzû) Grasping Two Stags
originLocation: Temple of Ninhursag, Tell al-'Ubaid, southern Iraq
medium: Hammered copper alloy sheets over bitumen and wooden core
creator: Unknown Sumerian temple metalworkers
anatomy: Roaring lion head projecting fully in the round
Outspread eagle wings and feathered raptor torso
Raptor talons clutching the rumps of two antlered stags
description: Excavated at the entrance of the Temple of Ninhursag at Tell al-'Ubaid, this monumental copper-sheathed lintel depicts Imdugud (Akkadian Anzû), the thundercloud bird and divine emblem of Ningirsu. Its three-dimensional roaring lion head projects boldly from the relief plane while its spread eagle wings and talons assert cosmic dominion over twin stags.

title: Votive Silver Vase of King Entemena Incised with Anzû
originLocation: Girsu (modern Telloh), Dhi Qar Governorate, Iraq
medium: Hammered and engraved silver on a copper base
creator: Royal workshop of Entemena of Lagash
anatomy: Frontal maned lion head on an eagle's feathered body
Outstretched wings and splayed tail plumage
Talons seizing pairs of lions and ibexes in heraldic symmetry
description: Dedicated by King Entemena of Lagash to the warrior god Ningirsu in the E-ninnu temple at Girsu, this finely chased silver vessel bears four repetitions of the lion-headed eagle Imdugud. Each emblem grasps pairs of lions, stags, or ibexes, illustrating the storm-bird's mediating power between celestial authority and earthly vitality.

title: Libation Beaker of Gudea with Mušḫuššu Dragons and Entwined Serpents
originLocation: Girsu (modern Telloh), Iraq
creator: Court workshop of Gudea, Ensi of Lagash
anatomy: Scaly serpentine-feline bodies standing bipedally with feathered wings
Horned viper heads, lion forepaws, and raptorial hind talons
Scorpion-tipped tails flanking a central staff of two entwined serpents
description: Inscribed by Gudea, ruler of Lagash, for his personal protective deity Ningishzida ('Lord of the Good Tree'), this dark green steatite libation beaker preserves one of the earliest canonical images of the horned Mušḫuššu dragon. Two winged dragon-chimeras hold upright standards flanking an axial caduceus-like staff coiled by mating vipers.

title: Apotropaic Terracotta Mask of Humbaba (Huwawa)
originLocation: Ur (Tell el-Muqayyar), southern Iraq
creator: Unknown Old Babylonian coroplast
anatomy: Grimacing monstrous face formed by convoluted, labyrinthine coils
Bared fangs and wide, staring apotropaic eyes
Visage evoking the divinatory coils of sacrificial entrails (tirānū)
description: In the Epic of Gilgamesh, the monstrous giant Humbaba guards the sacred Cedar Forest of the gods, terrifying intruders with his supernatural 'auras.' Old Babylonian clay plaques and masks render his grimacing face as a continuous, coiled line resembling sheep intestines examined in Mesopotamian extispicy omen rituals.

title: The Burney Relief ('Queen of the Night')
creature: Winged Talon-Footed Underworld Goddess or Lilītu
originLocation: Southern Mesopotamia, Iraq
medium: High-relief baked straw-tempered clay plaque with traces of pigment
creator: Unknown Old Babylonian sculptor
anatomy: Four-tiered horned crown of divinity and human female torso
Downward-swept multicolored raptor wings
Feathered bird-of-prey legs and talons perched atop two recumbent lions
description: Modeled in high-relief terracotta originally painted in brilliant red, black, and white, the Burney Relief portrays a naked, horned female entity with lowered raptor wings and bird talons standing upon two lions between flanking owls. Scholars identify this liminal nocturnal figure with Inanna-Ishtar in her underworld descent, her sister Ereshkigal, or the winged demoness Lilītu.

title: Monumental Sphinx Gate Guardian at Alaca Höyük
originLocation: Alaca Höyük, Çorum Province, Turkey
creator: Unknown Hittite imperial masons
repository: In situ / Alaca Höyük Museum, Turkey
anatomy: Human face framed by heavy Hathoric-inspired curled lappets
Massive leonine chest and forelegs carved into the monolithic jamb
Double-headed eagle relief carved on the inner flank
description: Flanking the ceremonial city portal at Alaca Höyük in central Anatolia, these two-meter monolithic stone sphinxes synthesize Egyptian Hathoric hair-curls with muscular Hittite leonine forms. As threshold guardians (Damnaššara), they protected the sacred precinct from malevolent forces while bearing imperial Hittite double-headed eagle emblems on their inner sides.

title: Boundary Stone (Kudurru) of Ritti-Marduk with Scorpion-Man and Mušḫuššu
originLocation: Sippar (Tell Abu Habbah), Iraq
dateDisplay: Reign of Nebuchadnezzar I, c. 1125–1104 BCE
creator: Babylonian royal scribes and sculptors
anatomy: Bearded human archer torso drawing a bow
Winged avian body with raptor talons
Segmented, curving scorpion tail and stinger alongside Marduk's horned dragon and giant coiled serpent
description: Granted by King Nebuchadnezzar I to the chariot commander Ritti-Marduk after a campaign in Elam, this limestone kudurru seals its legal curses beneath six registers of astral and monstrous divine emblems. Prominent among them are a bow-wielding Girtablullu (scorpion-man), Marduk's spade resting on a couchant Mušḫuššu dragon, Ea's goat-fish (Suḫurmāšu), and an overarching horned serpent.

title: Basalt Orthostat of a Winged Scorpion-Bird-Man from Tell Halaf
originLocation: Western Palace of King Kapara, Tell Halaf (ancient Guzana), Syria
creator: Workshop of King Kapara at Guzana
anatomy: Bearded human head with inlaid-style wide eyes and braided locks
Feathered avian chest and folded wings
Raptor talons and an upturned, segmented scorpion tail
description: Guarding the Scorpion Gate of King Kapara's palace at Guzana (Tell Halaf), this vesicular basalt guardian brings to monumental architectural life the Girtablullu, the mythic scorpion-men who guard the twin peaks of Mount Mashu at the rising and setting of the sun in the Epic of Gilgamesh. Shattered during World War II bombing in Berlin, the sculpture was painstakingly reassembled from hundreds of basalt fragments.

title: Colossal Human-Headed Winged Lion (Lamassu) from Nimrud
originLocation: Northwest Palace of Ashurnasirpal II, Nimrud (ancient Kalhu), Iraq
dateDisplay: Reign of Ashurnasirpal II, c. 883–859 BCE
creator: Royal Assyrian palace sculptors
repository: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (32.143.1)
anatomy: Bearded royal human head wearing a horned polos of divinity
Sweeping eagle wings and scaled breast plumage
Muscular five-legged lion body (stationary from the front, striding in profile)
description: Standing over three meters tall at a gateway of Ashurnasirpal II's Northwest Palace at Kalhu, this alabaster guardian fuses human intelligence, avian swiftness, and leonine ferocity into an apotropaic threshold spirit. Assyrian sculptors endowed the monolith with five legs so that viewers approaching straight on saw the beast standing firm, while those passing through the doorway saw it striding purposefully alongside them.

title: Palace Relief of an Eagle-Headed Winged Apkallu Sage
originLocation: Northwest Palace of Ashurnasirpal II, Nimrud (Kalhu), Iraq
creator: Royal Assyrian palace sculptors
anatomy: Hooked raptor beak, crested plumage, and curled mane
Four spread feathered wings radiating from a muscular human body
Ritual mullilu purifier cone and banduddû bucket held in human hands
description: Carved in crisp low relief across the ceremonial halls of Nimrud and inscribed down the midsection with Ashurnasirpal II's 'Standard Inscription,' this eagle-headed Apkallu represents one of the antediluvian supernatural sages sent by Ea to civilize humanity. Bearing a ritual bucket (banduddû) and purifier cone (mullilu), the winged spirit perpetually sanctifies the king and the sacred palace.

title: Dual-Headed Winged Chimera Orthostat from the Herald's Wall
originLocation: Herald's Wall, Carchemish, Gaziantep Province, Turkey
creator: Luwian-Hittite sculptors of Carchemish
anatomy: Conjoined bearded human head wearing a horned helmet and roaring lion head
Sickle-curved feathered wings rising from a striding lion body
Tail terminating in an upright, open-jawed bird or serpent head
description: Excavated along the ceremonial Herald's Wall at Carchemish on the Euphrates, this Neo-Hittite orthostat represents a direct Near Eastern forerunner of the Greek Chimera myth. Striding fiercely to the right, the winged leonine monster sprouts both a horned human head and a roaring lion's jaws from its shoulders, while its tail ends in a third biting zoomorphic head.

title: Luristan Bronze Standard Finial of the Hybrid Master of Animals
originLocation: Lorestan Province, Zagros Mountains, western Iran
creator: Unknown nomadic Luristan bronzesmith
repository: Harvard Art Museums (Arthur M. Sackler Museum), Cambridge, MA
anatomy: Janus-faced horned anthropomorphic demon-deity with multiple stacked faces
Sinuous, heraldically confronted felines with dragon-like necks
Secondary bird-of-prey heads projecting from the hip joints
description: Cast by the lost-wax method for the elite warrior graves of the central Zagros highlands, this tubular bronze finial exemplifies the surreal, metamorphic aesthetic of Iron Age Luristan. A horned, multi-faced supernatural 'Master of Animals' throttles two confronted long-necked feline monsters whose haunches sprout secondary raptor heads.

title: Neo-Assyrian Bronze Exorcism Plaque Against Lamashtu ('Plaque of the Hells')
originLocation: Northern Mesopotamia / Syria
creator: Unknown Neo-Assyrian āšipu-commissioned metalworker
anatomy: Roaring lioness head with donkey ears atop a hairy female body
Raptor talons kneeling on a donkey within a marsh-boat while suckling a piglet and puppy
Serpents clutched in each hand, overseen by the rival demon Pazuzu driving her back to the underworld
description: Hung beside the bed of a sick patient or expectant mother, this multi-register bronze exorcism plaque marshals protective spirits and the wind-demon Pazuzu to expel Lamashtu, the dreaded Mesopotamian child-snatching demoness. In the lowest register, lion-headed, talon-footed Lamashtu clutches twin vipers while suckling a pig and dog aboard a donkey-borne bark floating back down the subterranean river to the underworld.

title: Colossal Human-Headed Winged Bull (Lamassu) from Dur-Sharrukin
originLocation: Palace of Sargon II, Dur-Sharrukin (modern Khorsabad), Iraq
dateDisplay: Reign of Sargon II, c. 713–706 BCE
creator: Royal workshops of Sargon II
anatomy: Crowned human head with intricately curled Assyrian royal beard and bovine ears
Single sweeping sickle-shaped eagle wing with tiered feathers
Colossal four-meter bull body with stylized belly curls and cloven hooves
description: Towering over four meters high and weighing nearly thirty tons, this monumental alabaster bull-colossus guarded the royal citadel gates of Sargon II's newly founded capital, Dur-Sharrukin. Unlike earlier five-legged Nimrud guardians, Sargon's sculptors rendered the Khorsabad Lamassu with four stationary legs and a slightly turned head, projecting serene, immovable imperial majesty.

title: Urartian Gilt-Bronze Winged Bull-Lion Throne Figurine
originLocation: Rusahinili (modern Toprakkale, near Van), eastern Turkey
medium: Cast bronze with traces of gold leaf and stone inlay sockets
creator: Urartian royal court bronzesmiths
anatomy: Human face recessed for white and dark stone inlays beneath a horned polos
Upcurved feathered bronze wings originally covered in gold foil
Recumbent leonine-taurine body supporting a structural throne strut
description: Originally forming a load-bearing element of a sumptuous royal or divine throne in the Urartian temple-fortress at Toprakkale (Rusahinili), this cast-bronze hybrid merges human, avian, and bovine-leonine traits. Deep cells on the face and wings once held contrasting stone or glass paste inlays and gold leaf, showcasing the technical brilliance of Highland Anatolian metallurgy.

title: Cultic Basalt Water Basin with Fish-Cloaked Apkallu Sages
originLocation: Temple of Ashur, Assur (Qal'at Sherqat), Iraq
creator: Royal sculptors of Sennacherib
anatomy: Bearded human sages clad from head to calf in full-body scaled carp skins
Gaping fish head forming a mitre-like hood above the human brow
Caudal fins hanging down the back while holding purification buckets
description: Carved on the exterior of King Sennacherib's basalt lustration basin from the courtyard of the Temple of Ashur, pairs of fish-cloaked Apkallu flank the freshwater god Ea with flowing vases. Remembered in Berossus's Babyloniaca as the amphibious sage Oannes who rose from the Persian Gulf to teach humanity writing, arts, and law, these abyssal spirits embodied the primordial wisdom of the Apsû.

title: Inscribed Neo-Assyrian Bronze Statuette of Pazuzu
creature: Pazuzu (King of the Evil Wind Demons)
originLocation: Mesopotamia, Iraq
medium: Cast bronze statuette with cuneiform dorsal inscription (MNB 467)
creator: Unknown Mesopotamian metalworker
anatomy: Snarling canine-leonine face with bulging eyes and goat-like horns
Emaciated ribcage, four feathered wings, lion paws, and eagle talons
Scorpion tail and serpentine phallus
description: Inscribed in cuneiform across the back of its wings—'I am Pazuzu, son of Hanpa, king of the evil wind-spirits that issue violently from the mountains'—this fifteen-centimeter bronze statuette sports a suspension loop at the crown of its head. Though terrifying and pestilential himself, Pazuzu was invoked on domestic amulets to terrorize lesser demons and force his rival Lamashtu back into the netherworld.

title: Molded Glazed Brick Relief of a Mušḫuššu Dragon from the Ishtar Gate
originLocation: Ishtar Gate, Babylon, Babil Governorate, Iraq
dateDisplay: Reign of Nebuchadnezzar II, c. 575 BCE
creator: Royal brickmakers of Nebuchadnezzar II
anatomy: Horned viper head with forked tongue and elongated scaly neck
Lion forelegs paired with clawed avian hind talons
Long scaled body and upturned tail ending in a scorpion stinger
description: Set against a dazzling lapis-blue glazed brick ground along Nebuchadnezzar II's ceremonial Ishtar Gate, alternating rows of golden-white Mušḫuššu ('furious snake') dragons and storm-bulls guarded the northern entrance to Babylon. Sacred servant of the supreme Babylonian god Marduk, the striding composite beast combines viper, lion, eagle, and scorpion anatomy into an unmistakable emblem of divine kingship.

title: Glazed Brick Frieze of a Winged Lion-Griffin from the Palace of Darius
originLocation: Apadana Palace of Darius I, Susa (Shush), Khuzestan, Iran
dateDisplay: Reign of Darius I, c. 510 BCE
creator: Imperial Achaemenid craftsmen (Babylonian and Elamite brickmakers)
anatomy: Snarling lion head crowned with curved ibex horns and equine ears
Polychrome turquoise, yellow, and ivory sickle-curved wings
Lion forelegs paired with powerful feathered eagle hind legs and talons
description: Adorning the west courtyard of Darius the Great's palace at Susa, this molded siliceous brick frieze adapts Neo-Babylonian and Elamite glazing traditions into Achaemenid imperial court style. The striding monster unites a horned lion's head and forequarters with the hind talons of an eagle and jewel-like multicolored wings.

title: Double-Headed Eagle-Griffin (Homa) Column Capital at Persepolis
originLocation: Persepolis (Takht-e Jamshid), Fars Province, Iran
creator: Imperial workshops of Darius I and Xerxes I
repository: In situ, Persepolis World Heritage Site, Iran
anatomy: Fierce hooked eagle beak, prominent brow ridge, and upright mammalian ears
Crested neck mane with tightly carved scale-like plumage
Addorsed double-protome leonine-avian chests designed to cradle roof beams
description: Carved from polished grey limestone for an unfinished monumental hall or gate at Persepolis, these addorsed eagle-griffin column capitals are celebrated in Iranian tradition as representations of the auspicious mythic bird Homā. Combining raptorial beaks and crested manes with alert upright ears and leonine forequarters, the paired protomes epitomize the cosmopolitan synthesis of Achaemenid court sculpture.

title: Cult Relief of Nergal with Three-Headed Underworld Hound from Hatra
originLocation: First Temple, Hatra, Nineveh Governorate, Iraq
medium: Carved and painted Mosul limestone slab
creator: Unknown Hatran temple sculptor
repository: Iraq Museum, Baghdad / Mosul heritage record
anatomy: Three ferocious canine heads straining from a single collared body on a leash
Cobra-like serpents springing from the underworld god's belt and shoulders
Chthonic scorpions, lions, and standard-eagles crowding the sanctuary field
description: Excavated in the First Temple of the desert caravan metropolis of Hatra, this syncretic Parthian-era limestone relief portrays the Mesopotamian underworld god Nergal (syncretized with Heracles-Hades) clad in Iranian tunic and trousers. In his left hand he holds the leash of a snarling three-headed Cerberus hound while scorpions and serpents writhe across the chthonic threshold.

title: Sasanian Parcel-Gilt Silver Plate with the Royal Senmurv
originLocation: Iran (found in northern Iran / post-Sasanian Tabaristan tradition)
medium: Hammered, chased, and mercury-gilded silver dish
creator: Sasanian or Dabuyid royal silversmith
anatomy: Snarling canine-leonine head with protruding tongue and upright ears
Forward-curling feathered wings and clawed feline forepaws
Lush, foliate peacock tail symbolizing royal xwarrah (divine glory)
description: Wrought in repoussé silver highlighted with mercury gilding, this ceremonial banquet dish centers on the Sēnmurw of Zoroastrian cosmology, which nests atop the world-tree Harwisp-tōxmag and scatters the seeds of all plants with the beat of its wings. Combining a snarling dog-like muzzle, lion paws, upturned wings, and a sweeping peacock tail, the hybrid embodied Sasanian royal khvarenah (divine fortune).

title: Iskandar (Alexander) and the Talking Waq-Waq Tree
creature: Talking Tree of Waq-Waq (Zoomorphic Oracle Tree)
originLocation: Tabriz, northwestern Iran (Great Mongol Shahnameh)
medium: Opaque watercolor, ink, gold, and silver on paper
creator: Royal Ilkhanid scriptorium of Tabriz
repository: National Museum of Asian Art (Freer Gallery of Art), Washington, D.C. (F1935.23)
anatomy: Twin intertwined male and female trunks speaking by day and night
Branches terminating in living human women's heads and snarling animal muzzles
Raptors, foxes, felines, and horned beasts sprouting directly as foliage
description: Painted for the monumental Great Mongol (Demotte) Shahnameh in Ilkhanid Tabriz, this folio depicts Iskandar (Alexander the Great) reaching the edge of the known world to consult the prophetic Talking Tree. Its twin trunks blossom into scores of animated human faces and wild animal heads whose nocturnal voices foretell the conqueror's imminent death in a distant land.

title: Bahram Gur Fights the Karg (Horned Wolf)
originLocation: Tabriz, northwestern Iran (Great Mongol Shahnameh)
medium: Opaque watercolor, ink, and gold on paper
creator: Royal Ilkhanid scriptorium of Tabriz
anatomy: Single immense scimitar-like black horn curving from the brow
Massive lupine-leonine body with flame-like shoulder fur and striped coat
Clawed paws stretched out across a gnarled Chinese-inspired landscape
description: Among the supreme masterpieces of Ilkhanid manuscript illumination, this dramatic folio from Ferdowsi's Shahnameh shows the Sasanian king Bahram V (Bahram Gur) standing triumphantly over the slain Karg during his journey to India. Rendered with monumental vitality influenced by Yuan Chinese brushwork, the Karg fuses wolf, lion, and rhinoceros traits beneath a single lethal brow-horn.

title: Rustam Slaying the White Div (Div-e Sepid) in the Cave of Mazandaran
creature: Div-e Sepid (The White Demon of Mazandaran)
originLocation: Herat, Afghanistan (Baysunghur Shahnameh)
medium: Opaque watercolor, ink, and gold on paper
creator: Kitabkhana of Prince Baysunghur Mirza
repository: Golestan Palace Library, Tehran (UNESCO Memory of the World)
anatomy: Chalk-white pelted giant body with curved black horns
Fanged grimace, spotted demonic loincloth, and clawed hands and feet
Severed lower leg beside the pitch-black mouth of his mountain cavern
description: Created in 1430 in the royal Herat workshop of the Timurid prince Baysunghur, this celebrated miniature depicts the climax of Rustam's Seventh Labour in Ferdowsi's Shahnameh. Inside a pitch-black mountain cavern framed by blossoming trees and the bound guide Olad, the tiger-skin-clad hero plunges his dagger into the horned, white-furred chieftain of the Mazandaran demons to retrieve his liver blood and cure King Kay Kavus's blindness.

title: The Ascent of the Prophet Muhammad on Buraq (Mi'raj)
originLocation: Tabriz, Iran (Khamsa of Nizami for Shah Tahmasp)
medium: Opaque watercolor, gold, and ink on polished paper (Or. 2265, fol. 195r)
creator: Attributed to Sultan Muhammad
anatomy: Crowned human female face with delicate Safavid courtly features
Dappled equine-mule body adorned with a jewel-studded saddlecloth
Flaming golden halo and peacock-like tail soaring through lapis-blue Chinese clouds
description: Painted for Shah Tahmasp's royal copy of Nizami's Khamsa and attributed to the master Sultan Muhammad, this luminous folio portrays the miraculous night ascent (Mi'raj) of the veiled, flame-haloed Prophet Muhammad through a swirling lapis-lazuli sky. Bearing him past Gabriel and incense-offering angels is Buraq, envisioned in Persianate iconography with a crowned human countenance and swift piebald equine body.

title: Rustam and Rakhsh Slaying the Dragon (Third Labour)
originLocation: Qazvin / Tabriz, Iran (Shahnameh of Shah Ismail II)
medium: Opaque watercolor, ink, silver, and gold on paper
creator: Attributed to Sadiqi Beg
anatomy: Sinuous, scaled serpentine body with dorsal flame-spines
Four clawed limbs and horned, fanged East-Asian-inflected dragon head
Forked fiery breath opposed by Rustam's sword and the stallion Rakhsh's teeth
description: Attributed to the celebrated Safavid court painter Sadiqi Beg for the dispersed Shahnameh of Shah Ismail II, this dynamic folio illustrates Rustam's Third Labour. As the faithful stallion Rakhsh sinks his teeth into the scaly hide of the coiling Azhdaha, Rustam drives his blade into the monster's jaws amidst jagged violet and turquoise rocks.

title: Zal Returned to Sam by the Simurgh
creature: Simurgh (Benevolent Cosmic Phoenix of Mount Alborz)
originLocation: Qazvin, Iran (Shahnameh of Shah Ismail II)
medium: Opaque watercolor, ink, and gold on paper
creator: Attributed to Sadiqi Beg
anatomy: Flaming crest and jewel-toned crimson, turquoise, and gold wing plumage
Streaming ribbon-like tail feathers adapted from Ming feng-huang motifs
Powerful talons gently bearing the white-haired youth Zal from Mount Alborz
description: Abandoned in infancy on the crags of Mount Alborz because of his shock of white hair, the legendary hero Zal was raised in the eyrie of the wise, primordial Simurgh alongside her chicks. In this glittering Safavid folio from the Shahnameh of Shah Ismail II, the resplendent multicolored bird sweeps down through golden skies to restore the grown youth to his repentant father Sam, leaving Zal a single magic feather to burn in times of peril.
